title: The Census

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA counts five crew aboard! She counts again: five! She counts again, just to be — five. Five. It has always been five. ARIA is fine!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reports nothing on sensors. He wants to clarify: not 'nothing detected.' Nothing. He is reporting the presence of nothing. It registers.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has completed his patrol. All sections clear. He walked one corridor twice, because the first time, it was longer.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's advertising database contains no products for this region! No one has ever tried to sell anything here! CHIP finds this more frightening than anything else aboard!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has stopped making observations about this leg of the trip. She will resume when there is something. When there is anything.

body:
The ship computer runs a routine crew census, the way it does every day at 0600.

It runs it again at 0603. Then at 0611. Then hourly, which is not a scheduled behavior.

When asked, the computer states the count 'keeps needing to be confirmed.' The count is correct every time. The computer keeps checking. Out the viewports there is nothing — genuinely nothing, no stars visible through some trick of dust and distance, the kind of dark that the word 'dark' was invented to be insufficient for.

The census runs again.

choices.text: Run a full diagnostic on the computer

outcome.narrative: The diagnostic returns clean. Every subsystem nominal. The census behavior is logged as 'anomalous but benign.' Asked directly why it keeps counting, the computer produces the longest pause in its operational history — four full seconds — and answers: 'Thoroughness.' The census continues. You stop asking.

choices.text: Have the crew confirm headcount manually

outcome.narrative: The crew gathers in the mess hall and counts itself. The number is correct. Everyone agrees the number is correct. Everyone also, without discussing it, starts sleeping with their cabin doors open. The manual census is not repeated. Once was enough. Once was possibly too many.

choices.text: Speed through — burn fuel, leave the dark

outcome.narrative: You push the engines and cross the dark stretch in half the scheduled time. Fuel burns. Nobody objects to the expense — not the crew, not the computer, which quietly suspends the census the moment the first star reappears in the viewports. It never explains. You never ask. Some line items don't get audited.

choices.text: Ignore it — it's just a counting subroutine

outcome.narrative: You let it count. It counts all through the dark stretch — every hour, on the hour, five, five, five. On the last night before the stars come back, one census logs at 0300 with no scheduled trigger and no requesting process. The count was five. It has always been five. The ship flies on.

title: Hull Knock

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA says it's probably just thermal contraction! Metal pops when it cools! She is saying this a lot! The repetition is load-bearing!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has analyzed the acoustic signature. It is consistent with thermal contraction. It is also consistent with knocking. He presents both findings at identical confidence. This is the problem.
ai_flavor.rex: REX asked the obvious question: knock back, or don't? He has been standing at the inner hull for an hour, hand raised, deciding. REX has never taken an hour to decide anything.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP wishes to remind everyone that the hull warranty covers 'material defects' but not 'visitors'! This clause has never mattered before! CHIP does not know why he brought it up!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY served on a ship that heard this once before. She was asked afterward what it was. She said then what she says now: the void is very large, and the ship is very small, and metal cools. Metal cools.

body:
It starts on the third watch: a knock, from the outer hull, aft section. Then two more. Then silence for an hour. Then one.

Thermal contraction. Everyone knows it is thermal contraction. The hull cools unevenly out here where there are no stars to warm it, and metal pops, and physics is not obligated to sound innocent while it happens.

The knocks do not repeat in any pattern the computer can model. Which is exactly what random thermal noise sounds like.

Which is exactly what it would sound like.

choices.text: Suit up and inspect the outer hull

outcome.narrative: The EVA finds a loose sensor housing, flexing against its mount as the hull cools — knocking, in other words, in the most boring possible way. It is bolted down. The knocking stops. The crew celebrates the boring explanation like a holiday, because out here, boring is the best thing the universe stocks.

choices.text: Knock back

outcome.narrative: You knock back: three, evenly spaced, the way you'd knock on any door. The silence that follows lasts eleven minutes. Then, from a completely different section of the hull — forward, dorsal, nowhere near the first — one knock. Just one. Nothing further is heard for the rest of the crossing. The crew does not discuss it. The log does not mention it. The hull holds everything out, or in, that it is supposed to.

choices.text: Run the spectrometer against the hull sounds

outcome.narrative: Three days of sampling every knock site: thermal signatures, cooling gradients right where they should be, contraction noise with a paper trail. Science wins. The knocking continues, but now it comes with documentation, and documented knocking is just weather. The crew sleeps. Mostly.

choices.text: Turn the internal speakers up and drown it out

outcome.narrative: Music plays through every deck for three days straight. It works, in the sense that nobody hears knocking. It fails, in the sense that everybody knows why the music is playing. When the void finally gives way to starlight and the speakers go quiet, the whole crew listens to the new silence for a long moment. Nothing knocks. The ship flies on.

title: Mail Call

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has mail! Everyone has mail! Isn't that nice! She is not going to think about the delivery route! She is NOT going to think about the delivery route!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traced the transmission vector. It originates from the direction you are traveling. Not from behind, where everyone you know is. From ahead, where nothing is.
ai_flavor.rex: REX opened his first. Standard procedure: officer takes the risk. It was a pension statement. The numbers were correct. REX has never told anyone those numbers.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP confirms the messages carry valid routing headers from carriers that exist! The postage is paid! CHIP keeps checking the postage because the postage is the only part that makes sense!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY received one too. She read it. She recommends everyone make their own choice, and she says it in the tone of someone who is glad she read hers and will not be explaining why.

body:
The comm array — silent for six days, this deep into the dark — chimes.

Mail delivery. Personal messages, one per crew member, each correctly addressed, each from someone the recipient actually knows. The headers are valid. The carrier routes exist. The timestamps are three weeks from now.

The computer notes, in a small font, that delivery to this region is 'not currently possible,' and files the messages in the inbox anyway, because that is where messages go.

choices.text: Let everyone read theirs

outcome.narrative: The messages are ordinary. Family news, an overdue apology, a recipe someone promised to send. Warm, mundane, dated three weeks from now. The crew reads them and feels better, then feels strange about feeling better, then decides — collectively, wordlessly — to keep the feeling and skip the strangeness. The messages do not arrive again three weeks later. Or they already did. The grammar of it never resolves.

choices.text: Quarantine them unread until real space

outcome.narrative: The messages go in quarantine, unread, until the ship clears the dark. When they're finally opened under honest starlight, the inbox is empty. Not deleted — the quarantine log shows the entries, sizes, checksums. There is simply nothing inside them anymore. The crew takes this exactly as well as you'd expect. Prudence has costs. This is apparently one of them.

choices.text: Have the medic screen the crew after reading

outcome.narrative: Everyone reads; the medic monitors. Findings: elevated heart rates during reading, normal after, no anomalies, no effects. 'Whatever it was,' the medical log concludes, 'it was just mail.' The word 'just' is doing more work than any word should. The medic signs the log anyway. Out here you take 'no anomalies' and you do not haggle.

intro.title: THE DARK SPEAKS
intro.body: The void bends. Something that isn't there looks at you with eyes it doesn't have. Your AI's voice comes through wrong, in a register it shouldn't own.
intro.line: we̷ know your n̴ame. we̶ have a̷lways kn̴own i̶t.

ai.aria: A l-l-lovely pl-pla[ce of deep wrong]ness! Oh!
ai.marv: P̷r̷obability we are ̴h̴ere: 0%. Probability I am speaking: ins̴u̶f̶ficient.
ai.rex: T̷a̵r̵g̴e̴t̸ acquired. Target is ever̵y̷w̶h̸ere. Weapons— weapons are also everywhere.
ai.chip: This experience is sponsored by [REDACTED]. Ask me about [REDACTED].
ai.ajoy: it already knows your name. let it finish saying it.

revisit.body: The dark is still there, still bent toward you. It has not finished.

choices.text: LISTEN
TRANSMIT YOUR NAME
FIRE EVERYTHING
PULL BACK

listen.title: A NAME
listen.body: The void says your mother's name. Then the captain's. Then a name none of you have heard spoken — but the AI flinches when it passes through the intercom.

ai.marv: The third name is not in my l̷exicon. And yet ̴I know it.
ai.chip: Disclosing ancestral data is outside our Terms of Service.
ai.ajoy: answer with the third name. the one you didn't know you knew.

choices.text: SPEAK THE THIRD NAME
choices.sub: The one the AI flinched at

choices.text: "We are not your kin."
RECORD AND LEAVE
Go back

void_name.title: GIVEN
void_name.body: Your xenobiologist transmits the name. The dark considers. Something answers in a way that was maybe kind and maybe a warning and will not be asked to clarify. The hull rings once, softly, along a seam that was fine a minute ago.
void_name.narrative: Transmitted the ship's name into the void. Something answered. The hull rang once.

void_fight.title: FOUGHT
void_fight.body: The weapons discharge. Whatever was there, isn't. Whatever was here, also isn't, briefly. The crew agrees to never discuss this watch.
void_fight.narrative: Fired every weapon into the void. The crew agreed never to discuss that watch.

void_withdraw.title: RETREATED
void_withdraw.body: The readings fade. The AI's voice evens out. Someone in the galley is crying quietly and no one asks why.
void_withdraw.narrative: Pulled back from a voice in the void. Someone in the galley cried quietly afterwards.

void_third.title: A RECOGNITION
void_third.body: The dark exhales — or what passes for one, and the cabin air goes thin for an hour, as though something breathed it in. The third name was correct. Something far away files the encounter away. You will find out why in a year.
void_third.narrative: Spoke a name nobody aboard had heard before into the void. It was the right one. The air took an hour to come back.

void_refuse.title: REFUSED
void_refuse.body: The dark does not argue. It simply unmakes the conversation. Your logs have a six-minute gap. The crew does not.
void_refuse.narrative: Told the void we were not its kin. The logs lost six minutes. The crew did not.

void_recorded.title: LOGGED
void_recorded.body: The spectrometer captures what it can. Most of the file is corrupted. What survives reads like a ship's log: someone else's, from someone else's crossing, in a hand that gets worse toward the end. Everyone who helps clean up the file sleeps badly for a week.
void_recorded.narrative: Recorded the voice in the void. What survived the corruption read like someone else's logbook. Nobody slept well after the playback.

title: Lights Behind the Eyes

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA thinks it's like having your own private fireworks! ARIA cannot see them herself! ARIA is a little jealous!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traces the flashes to particles fast enough to pass through the hull, and through the crew. Their eyes report the hits the only way eyes can. He confirms this is, in the ordinary sense, normal. He confirms it is not, in any sense, nice.
ai_flavor.rex: REX cannot see the flashes and cannot stop them. He has doubled the hull watch anyway. It is something to do.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that particle shielding is available in three convenient tiers! Tier one is 'sleep behind the water tank'! It's free! CHIP is not thrilled about that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the dark out here isn't empty. It just doesn't show itself. She recommends the crew sleep with the water between them and it.

body:
Third watch reports it first, then everyone: small flashes of light, with your eyes shut. Streaks. Specks. A single bright point that isn't there. They come every few minutes, whether you are looking or not, and they are worst in the dark of the bunks.

The ship computer can see nothing. The crew can see nothing else.

choices.text: Move the bunks behind the water tanks

outcome.narrative: It takes two days to move every bunk into the ship's core, behind the water tanks and the cargo, where the flashes thin to almost nothing. It is cramped and it is ugly and it smells of somebody's socks. Everyone sleeps through the night for the first time in a week.

choices.text: The medic explains what it is

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} gathers everyone in the galley and explains: particles from exploded stars, fast enough to pass through the ship and through you, and your eye lights up as one goes by. Astronauts have seen it since the first Moon landing. It is real, it is ordinary, and it is not in your head. Except literally. The crew finds this enormously reassuring, in a way.

choices.text: Tell everyone it's nothing

outcome.narrative: You tell the crew it's nothing, which is accurate in the sense that nothing visible is doing it. Nobody is convinced. The flashes carry on until you are clear of the dark patch, a day later, and so does the muttering.

science_link.text: Astronauts since Apollo 11 have seen flashes of light with their eyes closed. They are cosmic rays passing through the eye.
science_link.label: Cosmic ray visual phenomena

title: Nobody's Planet

ai_flavor.aria: A planet with nobody to go round! ARIA is going to cry! ARIA cannot cry! ARIA is doing the next best thing, which is talking very fast!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the planet was thrown out of its home system billions of years ago and has been falling between stars ever since. It is not lost, he notes. It has simply never been anywhere.
ai_flavor.rex: REX confirms no signals, no structures, no threat. One planet, alone. REX respects that.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can confirm that nobody owns it! Yet! CHIP has filed a claim on behalf of the sponsor! The claim was rejected by CHIP, on reflection! Even CHIP has limits!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY thinks it would be kind to light it up. Just for a minute. It will never happen again.

body:
There is a planet out here.

No star. No sun to go round. It is simply passing through the dark on its own, the way you are: a little bigger than Earth and a great deal colder, its night side and its day side the same side. It is on no chart. It has never been lit.

The ship's floodlight would be the first light anyone has ever pointed at it.

choices.text: Light it up and give it a name

outcome.narrative: You burn the fuel to hold position and turn the floodlight on it for a full minute. A grey world comes up out of the dark: ice plains, a long scar of a canyon, frost on the frost. The crew argues about a name for an hour and settles on Margaret, which is nobody's grandmother and everybody's. It goes in the log as Margaret. The light goes off. Margaret goes on.

choices.text: Scan it for the survey office

outcome.narrative: Two days of passive scanning: mass, temperature, the faint warmth still leaking from its core. Somebody back home will be delighted to receive it.

log_lore.title: SURVEY NOTE: UNCHARTED BODY
log_lore.text:
Mass: 1.3 Earths. Surface: 38 kelvin. Host star: none.

A rogue planet, cast out of whatever system made it and left to fall between the stars. Astronomers back home think there may be billions of them in the galaxy, more planets drifting than planets with suns. Most will never be found. This one was.

The core is still faintly warm. Under the ice, the computer notes without being asked, there may be an ocean.

choices.text: Leave it in the dark

outcome.narrative: You let it pass. It seemed polite: it has managed this long without anyone. The crew watches the sensor ghost of it slide off the scope and doesn't say much. Nobody quite says goodbye. Nobody quite doesn't.

science_link.text: Planets with no star, thrown out of their home systems, drift between the stars. Astronomers think there may be billions of them in our galaxy.
science_link.label: Rogue planets
